newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Jordan says joining WTO will help mideast peace.
newsitem.headline: Jordan says joining WTO will help mideast peace.

text.p: Jordan, arguing its integration into the global economy would help strengthen the peace process in the Middle East, began negotiations on Monday to become a member of the World Trade Organisation.

But both Jordanian and WTO officials left no doubt they expected some tough discussions over the months ahead and that accession to the world trade body, which would ensure access to global markets, was unlikely to come before 1998.

"The world community, which has a stake in peace as much as the regional parties, is called upon to support those in the region....to be able to join the world economy," Jordan's Trade Minister Ali Abu-Ragheb told diplomats at the WTO.
"We need to show the average person in the street that peace indeed does have dividends," he added in an opening address to a WTO working party set up to study the Jordanian request.

Jordan is one of a total of 31 countries that now have applications pending to join the trade body, whose currently 124 members pledge to grant each other "most favoured nation," or equal and non-discriminatory, treatment.
Among Middle Eastern countries, applications are also under study from Saudi Arabia and Oman.
Israel, Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates are already members, but Western states recently blocked a bid from Iran to start the process.

Abu-Ragheb told reporters at a news briefing later that there was some opposition in his country to seeking membership, which would also mean Jordan would have to open up its markets for goods and services to foreign providers.
But the government was firmly convinced it was taking the right path.

"We in Jordan view the task of linking our economy to the global economy through membership in the WTO as a very important one, which we hope will ensure the entry of our goods and services, under the best conditions, to world markets," he told the WTO working party.
Jordan, which is in the process of a wide-ranging liberalisation of its national economy, will face considerable problems of adjustment in meeting WTO requirements for entry, the minister said.
For this reason, it was seeking entry as a developing country, which would allow it a longer period to bring all its trade-related regulations and practices up to full WTO requirements.

One problem the country would face in the future would be making up for the revenue losses as it began to lower import tariffs, which provide around one third of government revenues, he told the news briefing.

And in his speech to the working party, attended by trade envoys from Geneva missions to the WTO, he appealed for understanding and recognition that Jordan would have to approach new WTO commitments on a step-by-step basis.

"Let us hope that our accession to the WTO will be directed to support our internal efforts, and such new commitments not only will not aggravate the situation but through increased exports, will mobilise our resources to meet the already existing challenges without adding to them," the minister said.
